findings: Anteroposterior supine abdominal radiograph including the lower chest and pelvis

Sharply marginated, dense, teardrop-shaped radiopaque calcification in the right upper quadrant, projecting over the right renal fossa at approximately the level of L1-L2, with a smooth contour and homogeneous density, measuring approximately 2-3 cm in longest dimension
No additional discrete calcifications identified along the expected course of the ureters or in the bladder region
Lumbar spine demonstrates mild intervertebral disc space narrowing with marginal osteophyte formation at multiple levels consistent with degenerative change
Bowel gas pattern shows moderate faecal loading throughout the colon bilaterally; no definitive dilated bowel loops or air-fluid levels appreciable on supine projection
Pelvis and visualised femoral heads appear intact without focal lytic or sclerotic lesion
Soft tissue outline: no gross organomegaly definitively identified; right psoas shadow appears present; left psoas shadow partially obscured by overlying bowel gas
No pneumoperitoneum visible under the diaphragm on this supine view
Bilateral lower ribs and hemidiaphragms partially included; gastric fundal gas visible in the left upper quadrant
differential: Renal calculus (nephrolithiasis) — large, dense, smooth calcification in the right renal collecting system; the teardrop shape could represent a calyceal stone or early staghorn configuration
Gallstone — the right upper quadrant location and smooth dense opacity could represent a calcified gallstone, though the position appears more medial/inferior than the typical gallbladder fossa

Adrenal calcification — a calcified right adrenal gland lesion (e.g., prior haemorrhage, granulomatous disease) could produce a rounded/teardrop density in this location, though typically smaller and more superior
anatomyConcerns: The calcification projects over the right renal region but could overlap the gallbladder fossa depending on patient habitus; lateral or oblique views and/or cross-sectional imaging would be required to localise it to kidney, gallbladder, or adrenal
Supine projection limits assessment for free intraperitoneal air and air-fluid levels; erect or decubitus views would complement evaluation
Partial field-of-view at the superior margin limits full assessment of the lower chest and diaphragmatic contours
